summary: This unit teaches you to develop a business proposal that persuades a named reader to approve a course of action. You will learn the types of proposal (solicited, unsolicited, internal, grant and tender), how to research the reader's needs, how to structure the document, how to set out costs, benefits, payback and return on investment, how to plan the timeline and risks and prove you can deliver, how to write, review and present it, and how to stay honest and within the procurement rules.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is for supervisors and managers who write or review proposals: to win a contract from a ministry or a hotel, to win a grant for a community project, or to ask their own senior management to approve and fund an improvement. A proposal is a short, focused document with a clear request. Its job is to **persuade a named reader to approve a course of action**.

A proposal differs from a business plan. A **business plan** describes a whole business and how it will operate over several years. A **proposal** asks for a decision on **one offer or project**: this service, at this price, for these results, in this time.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Choose the right type of proposal
Tell solicited from unsolicited proposals, tenders, grant applications and internal proposals, and follow the rules of each.
Find out who decides, what they need, what worries them and how they will judge the proposals.
Write a summary, statement of need, solution, scope, objectives, timeline, costs, benefits, risks, evidence of ability and next steps.
Prepare a clear budget with contingency and GCT, and calculate payback, return on investment and benefit-cost ratio.
Show a timeline with milestones, list risks with responses, and prove you can deliver.
Use plain, persuasive writing, review with someone fresh, control versions, and present and defend the proposal.
Stay honest and within the rules
Follow the requirements of a request for proposals, protect confidential information, refuse improper gifts and treat all bidders fairly.
Make the contract terms clear when you win and use feedback when you lose.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenario and calculation questions (payback, return on investment, benefit-cost ratio, GCT and scoring).
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as RFP, tender, scope, contingency, feasibility) and essays.
**Practical group work**: writing a proposal that answers a request for proposals in full, and presenting and defending an internal proposal to a management panel.

blocks.note: Many marks come from small things: following the format given, working the figures twice and stating assumptions. A strong idea in a proposal that breaks the rules can be thrown out unread.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Type
What it is
Key points
rows: Written in reply to a request: the client has already accepted that there is a need
Follow the request for proposals (RFP) exactly: its format, page limit, order of sections, forms and closing date
Must first show that the need exists, and earn the reader's attention
A formal written offer to supply goods or services at a stated price, usually in reply to a public body's invitation
Strict rules; judged openly against stated criteria; late bids are normally rejected
Written for your own manager, board or committee, to approve an improvement or fund a project

Written to a funding body, such as a development fund, for money for a project

blocks.p: A **request for proposals (RFP)** is a document from a client, often a ministry, agency or municipal corporation, that states what it needs and how bidders must reply. It usually sets out requirements, a page limit, the order of sections, the evaluation criteria and the closing date. It is your instruction manual: read it several times, and list every requirement.

blocks.note: If the RFP says 10 pages and a fixed order of sections, **keep to the page limit and the set order exactly**. Evaluators score many bids on the same form. A bid that breaks the format may be marked down or rejected, however good it is.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: What every proposal needs to do

ul: Show that you **understand the reader's need**.
Offer a **clear solution** that meets it, with the scope stated.
Show **value**: why the offer is worth more to the client than it costs. This is the **value proposition**.
Show you can **deliver**: skills, resources and a track record.
Ask for a **specific decision** and say what happens next.

sections.title: Researching the reader and the need

blocks.p: Before you write, find out about the people who will decide. A proposal written without this knowledge is a sales leaflet.

blocks.h: Who and what to find out

head: Question
Why it matters
rows: Who decides, and who influences the decision?
You write for them. A board with no technical members needs plain explanations.
What are their needs, concerns and decision criteria?
The proposal must answer what they will use to judge it, such as price, experience, quality, speed or risk.
What is the problem in numbers?
Facts and figures make the need real: days lost, costs, complaints, errors.
What budget range and timescale do they have in mind?
Prevents wasted effort on an offer they cannot afford or on a date they cannot accept.
Staff, parents, students or the public may be affected and must be considered.
Procurement rules for public bodies, licensing, safety or data protection.

blocks.p: Gather data on current use, costs and problems before proposing a solution. For example, if a hotel group asks for a proposal to cut its water use, the writer must first find the current water bills, where the water goes and what has been tried, or the solution will be a guess. Meet the client where possible, and ask open questions. Agree how any personal or sensitive information will be protected.

Check that you can deliver: **Do we have the skills, time and money to deliver it?** A proposal that promises more than the firm can do may win the work and lose the money, and damages the firm's name.

If a proposal changes something that affects several groups, such as changing the supplier of a school canteen, which will affect students, parents and staff, the writer must show how each group's needs will be met. The decision makers will ask about each of them.

blocks.note: Write down the reader's decision criteria on one page and keep it in front of you. Every section of your proposal should score points on at least one of them.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use a logical order that a busy reader can follow. A common order is: **summary, need, solution, costs, next steps**, with the other parts placed where they help.

head: Section
What it does
Notes
rows: Names the proposal, the client, the writer and the date
Page numbers and headings help readers find things
The whole case in half a page: the need, the solution, the cost, the main benefits and the decision requested
At the front, so busy readers grasp the case quickly; **written last**, after the rest is drafted
Shows that you understand the problem, with facts
What the project will achieve, in SMART form
"Cut invoice errors by 50% within six months", not "improve invoicing"
What will be done, how and by whom
Include the options considered and why this one gives the best value
What is and is not included in the offer
Prevents disputes and extra unpaid work
A Gantt chart on one page
The budget, the benefits and the payback or return
Clear and honest; see the next section
What could go wrong and what you will do
Strongest proof that you can deliver
So the client can see the results
What the reader should do and by when
Detailed data, CVs, supporting documents, quotations

blocks.p: Use **SMART objectives**: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound. Compare a vague "improve customer service" with "reduce the average wait for service from 12 minutes to 8 minutes by 30 June".

A reader will wonder whether other ways exist. Briefly show other options you considered and why the chosen solution gives the best value. This builds trust. The reader sees that the writer weighed the alternatives.

Every price and forecast rests on assumptions, such as an exchange rate for imported items, the number of users, or the price of fuel. State them. If the assumption changes, the reader knows what happens to the figures.

blocks.note: For a quotation that includes imported parts, state **how long the quoted price is valid**. Exchange rates and supplier prices change, and an open-ended price can cost you money.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Costs, benefits and the financial case

blocks.p: A budget in a proposal must be complete and honest. Include not only direct costs (such as trainer fees, venue and materials) but also **staff time**, a **contingency** (a sum set aside for unexpected costs, often a small percentage), and **GCT** where it applies.

head: Cost line
J$
rows: Staff time (replacement cover while staff attend)

blocks.p: Show **GCT as a separate line**, worked out at the current rate, so that the client sees the price before tax and the tax separately. A quotation of J$720,000 for services is J$720,000 before GCT, and the GCT line is added to it. Do not quote a GCT figure unless you have checked the current rate.

List the benefits, and count what can be counted: money saved, income earned, time saved, errors avoided. Some benefits, such as better staff morale, are harder to measure. Describe them clearly, with evidence such as a survey or an example, and place them beside the costs in the cost-benefit section. Do not leave them out because they cannot be priced, and do not invent figures for them.

head: Measure
Formula
Meaning
rows: Cost ÷ net saving or net gain each period
How long until the cost is recovered
The net gain as a percentage of the cost
Above 1 means the benefits are greater than the costs

blocks.p: A stock-control system costs J$2,250,000 and is expected to save J$750,000 a year for four years.

ol: Total savings over four years = 4 × 750,000 = J$3,000,000.

blocks.p: Present the case in a small table that shows the cost in year 0, the saving each year and the running total, so the reader sees the point where the system pays for itself. A bar chart suits a comparison of the costs of three options; a line graph suits a running total over time.

blocks.note: Be careful with ROI: if a project costs J$1,600,000 and brings in J$2,000,000 of extra profit **before** its own cost is taken off, the net gain is J$400,000 and the ROI is 25%, not 125%.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: If the savings depend on something uncertain, such as future fuel prices, show the results if it rises or falls. This **sensitivity** check shows the reader how safe the case is. Work every calculation twice, and make sure that figures in the summary match those in the budget.

blocks.note: If a board member says the proposal costs too much, show the benefits and payback, and offer options such as a smaller first phase, rather than just cutting the price.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Timeline, risks and proof that you can deliver

blocks.p: A **Gantt chart** shows the stages of a proposed project as horizontal bars across a timeline, on one page. A **milestone** is a key point showing that a stage is complete. The reader can check that your plan is realistic.

head: Stage
Weeks
Milestone
rows: Agree details and sign the contract

blocks.p: Show that you have thought about what could go wrong. For each risk, give the **likelihood, impact and response**.

head: Risk
Likelihood
Impact
Response
rows: A key person is ill during the project
A named deputy trained in the task
Order early; quote a second supplier
Costs rise because of the exchange rate
State the exchange rate used; quote a validity period
Involve users early; training and a help desk

blocks.p: The strongest proof is **results from similar past projects, with referees** the client can contact. Add short CVs of the key people, a description of the equipment and a copy of relevant certificates. Do not claim experience you do not have, or list referees who have not agreed.

Name the **indicators**, the **targets** and the **review dates**. For a staff training programme, an indicator might be the number of staff who pass a test, with a target of 90% by month three and a review at months three and six. The client will then know what it is paying for.

blocks.note: Where the proposal is for a community group applying for a grant, add the group's own contribution and any other support, and show how money will be controlled and reported.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Write for the reader in **plain language**: short sentences, everyday words, and technical terms explained simply, or put detailed technical material in an appendix.
Use **specific, factual statements**: "The plan cuts processing time by about a third" beats "The plan will greatly improve everything".
Avoid unprovable boasting such as "best in Jamaica".
Use headings, short paragraphs and numbered lists.
Use visuals that suit the purpose: a Gantt chart for the timeline, a bar chart to compare costs, a line graph to show a trend.

blocks.p: When replying to an RFP, make a checklist matching **each requirement to the page** where you answer it. Tick every item before you submit. Forms, signatures and certificates are requirements too.

ol: Plan the review time in the schedule from the start, not for the last night.
**Compliance review:** someone who did not write the proposal goes through the RFP line by line against the checklist.
**Content review:** does it read as the client would see it? Is the need understood, the solution clear, and the evidence convincing?
**Figures review:** a second person checks every calculation, and that the summary agrees with the budget.

blocks.p: Use a colleague who did not help to write it: fresh eyes find errors and gaps the writers no longer see.

When several people edit a proposal, keep **one master file** with a clear name and version number, and say who may change it. Send only the final version to the client. A proposal sent with last week's figures can cost a contract.

flow: Find out how long you have, who is on the panel and what each member cares about
Build a short talk around the need, the solution, the key figures, the main risks and your request
Agree who presents each part, and rehearse at least twice against the clock
List the hardest likely questions and prepare short answers with evidence
In the meeting, answer honestly; if you do not know, say so and promise to find out
End by repeating your request and the next step

blocks.p: If a panel member says that the proposal costs too much, do not argue. Show the benefits and payback, and offer options. If you are asked something outside your knowledge, say so and promise to find out. Never invent an answer.

Public bodies must buy goods and services fairly. The general aim of the procurement rules for public bodies is that **bids are judged openly against stated criteria**, with every bidder treated equally. This is why:

ul: Bids are judged **only** on the stated criteria, such as price, experience, method and staff.

A bid that arrives after the **closing date and time** is usually rejected, however good it is. If a tender closes at 4:00 p.m. on Monday and the courier arrives at 4:10 p.m., expect rejection. Plan to deliver early, and keep proof of delivery.
All bidders get the same information. Questions and answers may be shared with everyone.
Contacting evaluators privately to influence the result is not allowed.

blocks.p: The weighted score is each score multiplied by its weight, added up: 2.8 + 2.7 + 1.2 + 0.8 = 7.5. Use the weights to decide where to put the effort in the proposal: the heavier the weight, the more space and evidence it needs.

If an officer at the client hints that a 'gift' would help a proposal succeed, **refuse and report it through the proper channel**. Offering or accepting such payments is dishonest and can be a crime, and it can end your firm's chance of future public work. Declare any **conflict of interest**, such as a family tie with a member of the evaluation panel.

A proposal is the basis of a later contract. Every claim about experience, staff, results and prices must be **true and checkable**, and assumptions must be stated. Promising more than the firm can deliver may lead to disputes, penalties under the contract and a damaged name.

ul: Protect what the client shares with you. Do not use it for other purposes.
If the proposal contains the firm's own design or method, such as a booking-system design, **mark it confidential** and agree the terms for its use in writing.

If you receive information by mistake that belongs to a competitor, such as its price file sent to you in error, do not read or use it. Tell the sender, and where the rules require, the procurement office, and delete it.
Do not copy other people's work without permission or credit.

blocks.note: Refer to the law by its purpose: procurement rules for public bodies, contract law, data protection law and intellectual property law. Ask the client's procurement office or a legal adviser if you are unsure.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A client who accepts a proposal normally follows with a **contract or order that confirms the terms** before work starts: the scope, the price, the dates, payments and what happens if something changes. Check that the contract matches your proposal. Any change the client asks for after the proposal should be agreed **in writing**, with its effect on price and time stated.

Ask for **feedback**. Many clients, particularly public bodies, will give a debrief on how the bid was scored. Use it to learn: was it price, evidence, method or presentation? A win can hide weaknesses, such as a price set too low or promises that will be hard to keep. A loss often contains lessons about price, evidence or presentation.

flow: Compare your score with the criteria and with the winner's strengths, where known
Record what worked and what did not
Update your standard text, CVs, references and price build-up
Decide whether to bid for similar work again

blocks.p: Proposals cost a great deal of staff time. Learning from every one raises the success rate and avoids bidding for work you are unlikely to win. The purpose is learning, not blaming.

ul: explain the aim of a proposal and how it differs from a business plan.
tell solicited, unsolicited, tender, internal and grant proposals apart.
follow a request for proposals exactly, including page limits, order and closing date.
research the reader's needs, concerns and decision criteria.
structure a proposal with an executive summary written last, objectives, scope, options, timeline, costs, risks and evidence.
prepare a budget with staff time, contingency and GCT as a separate line.
calculate payback, ROI and benefit-cost ratio, and check each twice.
state assumptions and the validity of a quotation.
plan a timeline with milestones, and show risks with likelihood, impact and response.
prove I can deliver with past results and referees.
write in plain, specific language and use the right visual.
organise a review with a colleague who did not write the proposal, and keep version control.

terms: Business proposal
A document that asks a named reader to approve a course of action.
Request for proposals (RFP)
A client's document that sets out its needs and how bidders must reply.
Solicited proposal
A proposal written in reply to a request.
Unsolicited proposal
A proposal the client did not ask for.
Tender
A formal written offer to supply goods or services at a stated price.
Executive summary
The short section at the front that sums up the whole case.
Scope
The limits of what a proposal does and does not cover.
SMART objective
Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Value proposition
Why the offer is worth more to the client than it costs.
Contingency
A sum set aside in a budget for unexpected costs.
Payback period
The time taken for savings or income to recover the cost.
Return on investment (ROI)
Net gain divided by cost, as a percentage.
Benefit-cost ratio
Total benefits divided by total costs.
Feasibility
Whether a proposed project can realistically be done with the resources available.
Gantt chart
A chart showing project tasks as horizontal bars across a timeline.
Milestone
A key point showing that a stage is complete.
Appendix
The section at the back that holds detailed supporting documents.
Closing date
The date and time after which a tender will not be accepted.
Conflict of interest
A personal interest that could affect, or seem to affect, a fair decision.
Version control
Keeping one master file with clear version numbers so that the wrong version is not sent.

c1.title: A laundry bid for health centres
c1.text: A regional health authority publishes a request for proposals for laundering linen for its 12 health centres. The RFP sets a limit of 12 pages and a fixed order of sections. Proposals close at 3:00 p.m. on Thursday. It will score proposals on price (40%), experience (30%), method (20%) and staff (10%). Hanson's Laundry Services, a Spanish Town firm, scores itself 7 for price, 9 for experience, 6 for method and 8 for staff. Its first draft is 15 pages. The RFP asks for three referees from similar contracts, but Hanson's has only two.

c2.title: GPS trackers for a logistics firm
c2.text: A fleet manager at a Montego Bay logistics firm proposes fitting GPS trackers to the firm's vans. The equipment and installation cost J$1,440,000. The trackers are expected to save J$120,000 a month in fuel and overtime. The tracking service costs J$20,000 a month. The manager is writing an internal proposal for the directors.

c3.title: A youth skills grant in Hanover
c3.text: A community group in Hanover is applying to a development fund for a six-month training course for young people. Costs are: trainers J$600,000; equipment J$450,000; venue J$180,000; materials J$150,000; and administration J$120,000. The group will add a 5% contingency on the total. The fund pays up to 80% of the total request and the group must raise the rest. The fund has said it wants proof that applicants can manage money.

c4.title: Pitching a guest-feedback system to a hotel
c4.text: A small firm has been shortlisted to present a guest-feedback system to the management committee of a hotel. The written proposal covers installation, training and a monthly service. The proposal's scope does not include staff training for night staff. At a pre-meeting, the hotel's manager says, "Can you add night-staff training as well? We can settle the price later." A committee member has already said that some guests do not use smartphones.

c5.title: A bid with a mistake and a loss
c5.text: A catering firm in Kingston is bidding for a ministry's staff-lunch contract. Its administrator receives an email, sent in error by the ministry's procurement clerk, with the price file of another bidder attached. The director of the catering firm also remembers that her cousin sits on the evaluation panel. The firm later loses the bid. The debrief says its price was 20% above the winner's, though it scored highest on quality.

questions.q: Hanson's first draft is 15 pages. What should the firm do?
o: Send the 15 pages with a note asking for leniency
Tighten the writing to fit within 12 pages
Shrink the print size so that it appears as 12 pages
Put the extra three pages in a second envelope
questions.why: The page limit is a requirement that all bidders must meet. Evaluators score on the same terms, so a bid that breaks the format may be marked down or rejected. Shorten the text instead.

questions.q: What is Hanson's weighted score out of 10?
questions.why: Price 7 × 0.4 = 2.8; experience 9 × 0.3 = 2.7; method 6 × 0.2 = 1.2; staff 8 × 0.1 = 0.8. Total = 7.5. The weights add up to 100%, so the total stays on the scale of 10. 30 is the sum of the scores.

questions.q: What is the best plan for meeting the Thursday 3:00 p.m. closing time?
o: Submit on Wednesday and keep proof of delivery
Deliver at 2:55 p.m. on Thursday to use all the time
Phone the office on Thursday to say it is on the way
Send it by courier on Thursday morning
questions.why: Late bids are normally rejected, and traffic or delays can strike at any time. Delivering early and keeping a receipt leaves a safety margin and proof.

questions.q: The RFP asks for three referees but Hanson's has only two similar contracts. What should it do?
o: Invent a third referee from a much smaller job
List a friend who has never used the firm's service
Name two real referees and add other experience
Leave the section out so that nothing looks missing
questions.why: A proposal must be true and checkable. Giving two honest referees with other relevant experience is better than a false claim that can be found out and ruin the bid.

questions.q: What is the net monthly saving from the trackers?
questions.why: The tracking service is a running cost, so net saving = 120,000 − 20,000 = J$100,000 a month. Ignoring the service fee gives J$120,000, which overstates the benefit.

questions.q: What is the simple payback period on the J$1,440,000?
o: 14.4 months
12 months
7.2 months
16.8 months
questions.why: Payback = cost ÷ net monthly saving = 1,440,000 ÷ 100,000 = 14.4 months. Check: 14.4 × 100,000 = 1,440,000. Using the gross saving of 120,000 would give 12 months.

questions.q: Over three years (36 months), what is the return on investment?
questions.why: Net benefit over 36 months = 36 × 100,000 = 3,600,000, less the cost of 1,440,000 = 2,160,000. ROI = 2,160,000 ÷ 1,440,000 × 100 = 150%. 250% would use total benefits (3,600,000) instead of net gain.

questions.q: Which visual best shows the running net saving month by month crossing the cost?
o: A pie chart
A line graph
A bar chart comparing three options
A table of the vans' registration numbers
questions.why: A line graph shows a trend over time, and the point where the line crosses the cost shows payback. A pie chart shows shares and a bar chart of options compares totals.

questions.q: What is the group's total request including contingency?
How much must the group raise itself?
If the fund agreed to pay 90% of the total request instead, how much would the group need to raise?
questions.why: 10% of the total request of 1,575,000 is J$157,500. Check: 90% of 1,575,000 = 1,417,500, and 1,575,000 − 1,417,500 = 157,500. J$126,000 wrongly takes 10% of the fund's present payment.

questions.q: What best answers the fund's wish for proof that applicants can manage money?
o: A statement that the group is honest and reliable
A promise to employ an accountant if it wins the grant
A longer description of the training course content
Past project accounts and a spending-control plan
questions.why: Evidence of past financial management and clear controls proves ability. A claim of honesty or a promise to hire later does not show it, and a longer course description does not answer the question.

questions.q: The hotel manager asks, "Can you add night-staff training? We can settle the price later." What should the firm do?
o: Accept it verbally and sort out the price after the contract starts
Refuse, because the scope was fixed in the proposal
Add it to the work and hope the price is agreed later
Agree a change in writing, with its price and timeline
questions.why: Changes to scope should be written down with their effect on price and time, so that both sides know what is included. A verbal promise leads to disputes and unpaid work.

questions.q: A committee member asks whether guests without smartphones can use the system. What is the best reply?
o: Say that almost everyone has a smartphone these days
Agree, and show how paper cards will cover them
Promise to look into it after the contract is signed
Say that the question is outside the proposal's scope
questions.why: A good answer deals with the objection honestly, with a practical solution. Dismissing it or postponing it suggests the team has not thought about the users.

questions.q: What should the team do to prepare for the presentation?
o: Read the whole written proposal aloud to the committee
Wait to see which questions are asked on the day
Rehearse against the clock and list hard questions
Ask the hotel for the questions in advance and use the answers
questions.why: Rehearsing against the clock keeps to the time given, and preparing for the hardest likely questions allows short, evidence-based answers. Reading the document aloud wastes the panel's time.

questions.q: How should the presentation end?
o: By repeating the request and the next step
With a long list of thanks to the hotel's staff
With a new idea that was not in the proposal
With an apology for any weaknesses in the proposal
questions.why: The end of a proposal presentation is a call to action: the decision requested and what happens next. New ideas confuse the panel and apologising weakens the case.

questions.q: The administrator opens the email and sees another bidder's price file. What should the firm do?
o: Stop reading, tell the sender and delete the file
Use the prices to lower its own price by a small amount
Keep the file in case the prices are needed later
Send the file to its own director for a quick look
questions.why: Information that belongs to a competitor and arrived by mistake must not be used. Telling the sender and deleting protects the firm and keeps the bidding fair. Using it could be dishonest and could disqualify the firm.

questions.q: What should the director do about her cousin on the evaluation panel?
o: Say nothing, as the cousin will surely be fair
Ask her cousin privately to support the bid
Withdraw the bid without telling anyone why
Declare the link to the ministry in writing
questions.why: A conflict of interest, or the appearance of one, must be declared so that the ministry can decide how to handle it. Hiding it or asking for support damages the fairness of the process.

questions.q: What is the best lesson to record from the debrief?
o: Lower the quality in the next proposal so that the price falls
Review its price build-up and whether to bid again
Blame the evaluators for not valuing quality
Stop bidding for work from public bodies
questions.why: A loss with a high quality score and a high price points to the cost build-up and to whether the work suits the firm. Cutting quality and blame do not help, and giving up forgets that learning raises later success.

questions.q: Benefits of J$1,260,000 are expected for a project that costs J$900,000. What is the benefit-cost ratio?
questions.why: Benefit-cost ratio = total benefits ÷ total costs = 1,260,000 ÷ 900,000 = 1.4. Check: 1.4 × 900,000 = 1,260,000. A ratio above 1 means the benefits exceed the costs.
